body:
### Summary

### Summary

On Windows 11 with Smart App Control enabled, Python executables supplied by uv-managed Python installations are unsigned and are being blocked by Windows Application Control.

This also affects virtual environments created from those Python installations because their `Scripts\python.exe` executables are unsigned.

For example:

```cmd
C:\Users\<user>>C:\Users\<user>\.venvs\automation-lib\Scripts\python.exe --version
Unable to create process using 'python  --version': An Application Control policy has blocked this file.
```

PowerShell reports that the virtual environment's executable is not signed:

```powershell
$p = "C:\Users\<user>\.venvs\automation-lib\Scripts\python.exe"
Get-AuthenticodeSignature -LiteralPath $p |
    Select-Object Status, @{n="Signer"; e={$_.SignerCertificate.Subject}}, Path
```

Output:

```text
Status : NotSigned
Signer :
Path   : C:\Users\<user>\.venvs\automation-lib\Scripts\python.exe
```

The same executable was also blocked when an IDE attempted to load it. Windows Security reported:

```text
Part of this app has been blocked

Some features of Wing Pro may not work because we can't confirm who
published python.exe that the app tried to load.
```

These environments had worked previously. Smart App Control began blocking them on October 23, 2026.

I confirmed that this is related to the executable rather than the location of the virtual environment:

1. Affected environments were based on uv-managed Python installations under `C:\tools\uv\python`.
2. Their Python executables reported `NotSigned`.
3. I installed the corresponding signed CPython release from Python.org.
4. I rebuilt the virtual environment using that system Python.
5. The rebuilt environment works from both `cmd.exe` and Wing Pro.
6. Its executable has a valid Authenticode signature.

For example, after rebuilding:

```cmd
(default313) C:\>python --version
Python 3.13.15
```

The location of the working environment remains under:

```text
C:\Users\<user>\.venvs
```

Therefore, moving the environment outside the user profile does not appear to be necessary. The material difference is whether the Python executable used to create the environment is signed and accepted by Windows Application Control.

The affected environments were created with uv 0.12.5 or an earlier uv release. I subsequently upgraded to uv 0.13.5, but upgrading uv itself does not replace unsigned Python executables already present in existing environments.

### Expected behavior

A Python installation managed by uv, and virtual environments created from it, should be usable on a standard Windows 11 installation with Smart App Control enabled.

Ideally, Windows executables distributed through uv-managed Python installations would carry an Authenticode signature trusted by Windows.

If signing these executables is outside uv's control because they originate from `python-build-standalone`, it would be helpful for uv to:

- document the compatibility issue;
- explain how users can select a signed system Python instead; and
- consider warning Windows users when a managed Python executable is unsigned.

### Actual behavior

Windows Smart App Control blocks the uv-managed Python executable and reports:

```text
An Application Control policy has blocked this file.
```

This prevents Python from running directly and prevents development tools such as Wing Pro from using the affected environment.

### Additional configuration

As a workaround, I installed signed Python.org builds and set:

```text
UV_PYTHON_PREFERENCE=only-system
```

I then rebuilt the affected environments using those system Python installations. The rebuilt environments work normally.

### Platform

Windows 11 Pro 25H2 (OS build 26200.9711), x86_64

### Version

uv 0.13.5 (46776a95d 2026-10-21)

### Python version

Python 3.13.15
title: Windows Smart App Control blocks unsigned uv-managed CPython and venv executables
